summary: Jesus calls Himself the door of the sheep and the good shepherd who lays down His life and takes it up again, and the crowd divides over Him.
key_insight: Jesus spoke these words to the same Pharisees who had just thrown the healed blind man out of the synagogue (9:34, 40). They had cast out a sheep; the Good Shepherd went and found him. The contrast between shepherd and hireling was not abstract.
story: Still speaking to the Pharisees who had cast out the man born blind, Jesus said, “Most assuredly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door, but climbs up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.” The shepherd comes in by the door. The doorkeeper opens to him, and “the sheep hear his voice; and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.” He goes ahead of them, and they follow him, but they will run from a stranger. His hearers did not understand what He was telling them.

So Jesus said again, “I am the door of the sheep.” All who came before Him were thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them. “I am the door. If anyone enters by Me, he will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture.” The thief comes only to steal, to kill and to destroy. “I have come that they may have life, and that they may have it more abundantly.”

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives His life for the sheep.” A hired man who does not own the sheep sees the wolf coming and runs, and the wolf scatters the flock, because the hireling does not care about the sheep. “I am the good shepherd; and I know My sheep, and am known by My own.” As the Father knows Him and He knows the Father, so He lays down His life for the sheep.

He has other sheep that are not of this fold, and He must bring them too. “They will hear My voice; and there will be one flock and one shepherd.” The Father loves Him because He lays down His life in order to take it again. “No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of Myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.”
Again the Jews were divided. Many said, “He has a demon and is mad. Why do you listen to Him?” Others said, “These are not the words of one who has a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”

scene.label: The sheepfold
scene.text: A fold was a stone-walled pen, sometimes a courtyard beside a house, where flocks were kept at night. Several flocks might share one fold under a doorkeeper; in the morning each shepherd called, and his own sheep came out to him. In open country, shepherds have been described lying across the opening of the fold, so that nothing could go in or out except past them.

scene.label: Israel’s shepherds
scene.text: Kings and leaders were called shepherds. Through Ezekiel, God condemned shepherds who fed themselves and scattered the flock, and promised to seek His sheep Himself and set over them one shepherd, “My servant David” (Ezekiel 34:1–23; compare Jeremiah 23:1–4).

scene.label: The hireling
scene.text: A hired hand was paid by the day and had no stake in the flock. David, by contrast, went after a lion and a bear to rescue a single lamb (1 Samuel 17:34–35).

scene.label: Other sheep
scene.text: God had promised through Isaiah to gather “others besides those who are gathered to him” (Isaiah 56:8). Jesus’ “other sheep” are those outside Israel’s fold, the Gentiles who would hear His voice.

witnesses.john: Only John records this teaching, and he ties it to the man born blind, who heard Jesus’ voice and worshiped Him after the leaders cast him out (9:35–38; 10:21). It holds two of John’s seven “I am” sayings, the door and the good shepherd, and it speaks openly of the cross: the Shepherd lays down His life and takes it up again by His own authority.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the Shepherd God promised. He knows His sheep by name, goes ahead of them, and dies for them by His own choice; no one takes His life from Him, and He takes it up again.
seeing.living: The sheep know the Shepherd by His voice. Learn His voice in His word, so that you can tell it from the voices that come only to take from you. If you belong to Him, He knows your name, and He has already laid down His life for you.
seeing.ponder: Whose voice have you been following lately, and does it sound like the One who laid down His life for you?

preaching.big_idea: The Good Shepherd knows His sheep by name and freely lays down His life for them.
outline: The shepherd who dies for the sheep (11–15)
One flock, and a life taken up again (16–18)
preaching.watch_for: Five times Jesus says He gives or lays down His life (vv. 11, 15, 17, 18 twice). The center of the passage is not the sheep’s duty but the Shepherd’s death, freely chosen and followed by resurrection.
